column3: Beyond Data is a siting tool for urban data centres in Vancouver and Edmonton. Data centres already sit in our cities, taking power, water and land while giving back only digital services. The tool asks what else they could trade with their neighbours. A user picks a lot and sizes a data centre on it; the tool finds the nearby buildings and systems that could use its heat, power, water, materials and space, and what it could take from them in return. For each exchange it maps the parties involved, the costs, the grid and policy conditions, and what stands in the way, shown as ranges with their sources and how far to trust each one. It gives trade-offs, not verdicts: who an exchange works for, at what cost, and what would have to change. Three levels of detail serve residents, community decision-makers, and engineers and planners.

This project explores an adaptive office building that changes its spatial configuration in response to collective user needs. A fixed 12 × 24 metre core supports interchangeable 4 × 4 × 4 metre modules for focused work, meetings, experimentation, social interaction, and gardens. Users describe their needs through a conversational interface. AI interprets this feedback, while a demand multiplier simulates how shared preferences influence the building’s existing spatial priorities. Proposed changes appear in a 3D preview for review and confirmation. An underground rotating warehouse stores spare modules, and a mobile lifting structure retrieves, relocates, and returns them. A separate animation demonstrates the sequence of movements required to reach the proposed configuration. The project investigates architecture as an ongoing feedback process linking human preferences, computational decisions, and physical transformation. Through interactive simulation, it asks how collective demand can reshape shared workplaces while retaining human oversight and making the consequences of change visible.

Behaviour Sim brings everyday human activity into early architectural design. Architects provide a schematic floor plan, define room uses, and select occupants and daily routines. The tool simulates movement, waiting, occupancy, encounters, and gaze throughout a working day. Animated replays and spatial maps reveal congestion, capacity problems, and opportunities for interaction or privacy. Designers can revise layouts and compare alternatives under consistent conditions. AI supports research, plan interpretation, and development, while architects retain design judgment. Future work will compare simulation results with a real building and explore how individual accounts of simulated experiences can support clearer, more accessible design reviews.

Form Follows Program is an AI-assisted web tool that aim to help architects integrate environmental performance into early spatial design. Different activities require different levels of environmental protection, yet conventional workflows often address conditioning after spatial layouts are established.

In BC non-profit housing, churches and societies often pay for weeks of design before anyone checks the scheme against zoning, City policy, the tree by-law and funders' rules. The rules sit in forty documents, are checked by hand, and the version used goes unrecorded. First Look gives non-profit developers and their architects three answers for a site and option: is it allowed, outright or by rezoning? Does it fit the funders? What remains unsure, and who resolves it? A five-layer rule stack, dated and cited to public sources, drives a deterministic engine, checked by evaluation cases and three user sessions. Users get a memo showing its arithmetic, a version stamp and a Revit massing. The first attempt reproduces the City's referral-report numbers for 998 East 19th Avenue.

column3: Architects and landscape designers turn cultural motifs, photographs and briefs into screens and facade panels, but the path runs through one designer's head and a vendor's process: the meaning of the design stays in notes, rules stay implicit in a vector file, and picture-to-panel systems like Ombrae tiles or perforated imaging cannot be tried before an order. Pattern Studio is a single-file web tool that reads a pattern's symmetry from a photograph, reads a brief into editable settings showing what it understood, and builds one picture three ways (cut screen, tilted optical tiles, perforated image) with real stock gauges and fabrication checks in code. The model proposes a design, code clamps and checks the design, the person confirms and exports DXF, STL and a tile schedule with provenance attached. Four benches and five agents check it daily. For user sessions, a student designer, fabricator, and shop owner could create fabricable designs.

Today, architects designing high-rise buildings in Downtown Vancouver use separate documents and tools to assess regulatory requirements and environmental performance. This fragmented workflow requires rebuilding models across platforms and reveals conflicts late in design. The Tower Design Toolkit proposes a browser-based proof of concept connecting an expandable range of design and analysis tools through a shared project model. Designers can customize workflows across concept and research, form and program, schematic design and design development, revisiting decisions and running analyses at any stage. AI interprets requests and helps build tools, code performs calculations, while designers continue to develop and refine the design. Recognizing that no single tool suits every practice, the open-source system allows users to copy, adapt, and contribute tools to the shared library. Next, we will develop the shared data structure and test standard workflows with practitioners and students to evaluate usability and guide further development.

Planting design requires plant knowledge, site assessment, spatial composition, and decisions about how a place should work. Today, plant research, layout development, and revisions often happen across separate references and tools. General-purpose LLMs can suggest plants, but their supporting evidence and design logic are difficult to verify. Planting Intelligence proposes a public-facing AI planting design tool for community members, non-specialists, and designers. A sourced plant database and design-logic base would inform plant selection, spatial composition, and revisions. When goals conflict, the tool could compare alternatives and explain trade-offs. Users retain final choices, while unverified site conditions remain visible. The project will connect these knowledge sources to an LLM, check constraints with code, and compare results with and without retrieval. An initial rule-based prototype demonstrates traceable revisions using 12 plant records, 14 principles, and three predefined strategy types. The intended outcome is an editable, evidence-linked planting proposal.

Kwu Tung North 1982 digitally archives a non-indigenous village in Hong Kong that has been redeveloped by the Hong Kong government in 2024. It tells the story of the village through archival government data including orthographic aerial photos, LIDAR data, and reinterprets this through new texturing of what the village may have looked like. Users have the ability to walk through the village and see landmarks such as Hau Shek Ancentral Hall, shrines, Dill's Corner, Marriage barracks and Soy sauce factories.

NPC is a proof-of-concept tool that uses AI to bring subjectivity into building simulation. Most design-stage simulations, from energy to pedestrian movement, summarize a building through quantitative metrics. NPC instead evaluates a design through the eyes of many different occupants, each with their own preferences. Users start with a plan, a description of how the space is used, their design goals, and any special cases. The tool generates occupant archetypes from that description and a default set of parameters, then simulates a day in the space. As agents move through it, they comment on what they experience, and those comments are summarized into design suggestions you can trace back to the agent who raised them. New seeds produce new iterations. The current mockup uses the third-floor studios of the Lasserre Building at UBC. Future versions will accept any input geometry.

The Vancouver Site Screener is a city-wide tool that ranks every residential lot in Vancouver by its redevelopment profit potential under the 2026 pre-zoning rules. It combines City of Vancouver open data, BC Assessment values and the encoded zoning schedules to run a residual land value pro forma on each parcel: allowable floor area, revenue, land cost, construction costs, city fees and inclusionary housing requirements. Lots that are tax-exempt, implausible or built out are dropped, and the rest are ranked by margin on cost. The output is an interactive dashboard with a top-100 table, a margin map, filters by zone and street, and a flag for lots listed for sale, scored at their asking price. Every assumption is documented with its source and a confidence grade, so the numbers can be checked and challenged. It finds the lots worth a developer’s next half-day of design; it does not replace the design.

column3: In Vancouver, a site is redeveloped when its pro forma pays: what a new building earns, less costs and a required return, sets what the land can cost. Planners and housing advocates see the resulting displacement only afterward, and nothing links land profitability, policy and tenant loss. This tool lets a planner choose a site, set policy levers such as density, fees and protections, and see whether the site pays to redevelop and how many tenants leave, year by year. AI extracts rents, costs and fees from Council staff reports and drafts the case one sentence per result. A person checks each step and decides, and code stops wherever a source is missing. Inputs are sourced, the numeric model is kept apart from the sourced rules, and evaluation cases are checked without the model. A planner leaves able to show which policy shifts make redevelopment pay, and who is displaced.
